title: Job search and interviews
why: Projects get you shortlisted; interviews get you hired. Each stage of an AI engineering loop can be practised, so practise them on purpose rather than learning from rejections alone.
outcomes: A one-page CV built around three projects with numbers
A portfolio page linking live demos and case studies
A target list and a weekly application rhythm
Ready for coding screens, take-homes, system design and behavioural rounds
lessons: CV: one page, three projects with numbers (eval scores, latency, cost), domain story first
Portfolio: a GitHub profile README or simple site linking live demos and case studies
Target list: 40 employers across edtech, the public sector and data-heavy firms, AI-adjacent roles included
Coding screen: 30 easy and medium Python problems, timed
Take-homes: two mock take-homes of 6 hours each (a RAG app, an eval harness)
System design: practise the two design prompts in the question bank out loud, recorded
Behavioural: write six STAR stories (conflict, failure, ownership, influence, ambiguity, delivery)
Apply weekly: 5 to 8 targeted applications, logged in your notes
resources: Do the easy and medium arrays, strings and hashing sets
Optional; strong for system design rounds
method: Treat every rejection as data. Log the stage reached and the question that hurt, then fix that one thing that week.
build: CV, portfolio page, six STAR stories and your first 20 applications sent.

qs: Explain RAG to a non-technical manager.
One analogy, one sentence on why it beats a plain chatbot, one limitation.
How would you reduce hallucinations in a support bot?
Grounding, citations, a refusal path, evals that count unsupported claims.
Fine-tuning or RAG: when would you use each?
RAG for changing knowledge and citations; fine-tuning for style, format or narrow tasks. Often both.
How do you know an LLM feature is working?
Golden set, retrieval and generation metrics, human-label calibration, production tracing.
The provider returns 429s under load. What do you do?
Backoff with jitter, queueing, caching, rate-limit budgets, a fallback model.
Design question answering over 1 million internal documents.
Requirements first; ingestion, chunking, hybrid retrieval, reranking, permissions, evals, cost per query.
Design a support agent that can issue refunds.
Workflow versus agent, tool permissions, approval thresholds, audit logs, failure paths.
Answers got worse after a data update. Debug it.
Compare eval runs, check ingestion and chunk counts, retrieval recall, then prompts.
Why that chunk size?
Point to the experiment and the numbers, not a blog post.
What did your evals miss?
Name a real blind spot and how you would close it.
What breaks at 100 times the traffic?
Rate limits, latency tail, vector index size, cost; what you'd change first.
Tell me about a time data you delivered was wrong.
STAR: own it, the fix, the process change afterwards.
Influencing a stakeholder without authority.
Evidence you used, how you framed it in their terms, the outcome.
A project you'd do differently.
Specific decision, what you learned, what you now do instead.

quiz.e: It keeps behavioural answers specific and short.

o: Working, tested code, eval numbers and a README with trade-offs and limits
quiz.e: Reviewers grade judgement and clarity, not feature count.

quiz.q: First step in a system design interview:
o: Clarify requirements and constraints: scale, latency, data, users
quiz.e: Designing before clarifying is the most common failure.

quiz.q: 'Tell me about a project' should lead with:
o: The problem and impact, then decisions and trade-offs
quiz.e: Interviewers want judgement; the stack is supporting detail.

quiz.q: You don't know an answer. Best move:
o: Say so, reason aloud from what you do know, and say how you'd find out
quiz.e: Visible reasoning scores better than a confident wrong answer.
